source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
Forty megawatts at CyrusOne's Durham campus is 80 percent of all data center capacity North Carolina operators have disclosed, and 14 of the state's 19 mapped facilities disclose none at all.

The pattern is a disclosure gap rather than a construction gap. Five North Carolina facilities publish megawatt figures, and one of them, this two-building campus with 420,000 square feet of technical space, accounts for four fifths of the disclosed total. The state's real inventory is therefore mostly invisible, and the visible part is dominated by a single operator's spec sheet.

For AI, published IT capacity in megawatts is the closest public proxy for how much compute a site can host, which makes the missing 14 facilities a missing map of where AI capacity could sit. What Durham's 40 MW actually serves is unstated: the operator publishes no breakdown by workload or tenant class, so nothing here distinguishes general colocation from AI training. A derived estimate at 100 kW per rack implies roughly 400 racks, and at 40 kW per GPU with 8 GPUs per rack, about 1,280 accelerators, but that is arithmetic on an assumed density, not a published figure.

The specifications also omit the power side entirely. There is no PUE, no grid operator serving Durham, no power purchase agreement, and no certifications. Without those, 40 MW is a nameplate number that does not establish whether the campus can draw that load continuously or what the local grid permits. The suitability score of 69 rests only on published IT capacity and operator type, and flags announced expansion as the input it lacks.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
